westonbirt.intro: Westonbirt, The National Arboretum, sits about 5 km south-west of Tetbury in Gloucestershire, roughly 27 km north-east of Bath and 31 km from Bristol in a straight line, and a car is the realistic way in. Its oldest tree is not one of the famous plantings but a small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, coppiced for centuries and claimed at 2,000 years. In the Old Arboretum stand giant redwoods, the oldest documented pair planted in 1856, and one tree that has rooted its own branches into a ring of new trees.
westonbirt.meta_description: A small-leaved lime in Silk Wood claimed at 2,000 years and kept alive by coppicing, beside the 1856 gateway redwoods of Westonbirt Arboretum.
westonbirt.question_meta: Westonbirt Arboretum's oldest tree is a small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, claimed at 2,000 years and kept alive by coppicing. What is known and what is not.
westonbirt.question_answer: The oldest tree at Westonbirt Arboretum is the small-leaved lime in Silk Wood, which Forestry England calls the 2,000-year-old lime. It is a ring of about 60 coppice stems from one ancient stool, last cut in November 2012. Nobody has dated it, so the 2,000 years is the owner's estimate rather than a measurement.
westonbirt.question_context: A small-leaved lime normally lives about 500 years, according to the Friends of Westonbirt. This one has outlasted that, they say, because it has been coppiced again and again. Cut to the base every twenty years or so, it sends up a fresh ring of stems from the old roots. Forestry England describes the original tree as thought to be hundreds, possibly thousands, of years old, and coppicing in Silk Wood is recorded from 1292. The 2,000 figure is repeated by both the owner and the Friends but rests on no dating study, so treat it as a strong tradition. The lime's 2012 coppice became a sculpture by Richard Harris, and the next cut is due around 2032. Do not expect a tower. What you will find is a thicket of poles that happens to be one very old tree. The arboretum's other big names are younger and better documented. The giant redwoods at the original gateway were planted in 1856, according to Redwood World citing the Forestry Commission, and by 2010 the taller of them stood 38 metres.

faq.q: How do I get to Westonbirt from Bath or Bristol?
faq.a: Westonbirt is off the A433 about 5 km south-west of Tetbury, roughly 27 km north-east of Bath and 31 km from Bristol in a straight line. The nearest station is Kemble, about 12 km away, so a car or taxi is the realistic route. The arboretum offers discounted entry to visitors arriving by bus, train or bike.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to see the trees?
faq.a: Yes. Westonbirt charges for entry, about 14 to 22 GBP for an adult day ticket depending on season and day on its 2026 pages. It opens daily from 9am except Christmas Day, with last admission at 4pm, and booking ahead is advised in autumn.

faq.q: Can I bring a dog?
faq.a: Dogs on leads are allowed in Silk Wood, where the old lime stands, but not in the Old Arboretum, where the redwoods are.

stow-on-the-wold.intro: Stow-on-the-Wold's most photographed trees are two yews that have grown into a church door. They stand either side of the north porch of St Edward's, their trunks pressed into the stone frame, a couple of minutes' walk from the Square. Locals call it the Tolkien door, after a rumour, never confirmed, that it inspired the Doors of Durin. The churchyard is open and free, and the door is on the north side of the church.
stow-on-the-wold.meta_description: Two yews have grown into the north door of St Edward's, Stow-on-the-Wold, the rumoured Tolkien door. How old they are, what is known, and where to stand.
stow-on-the-wold.question_meta: The two yews at the north door of St Edward's, Stow-on-the-Wold, are about 300 years old by the civic society. The Tolkien rumour and the age dispute.
stow-on-the-wold.question_answer: The best-known old trees in Stow-on-the-Wold are the two yews flanking the north door of St Edward's church, roughly 300 years old according to Stow Civic Society. In 1897 an archaeological society already called them ancient, so the age is disputed. They are free to see in the open churchyard.
stow-on-the-wold.question_context: Stow Civic Society says the north porch of St Edward's was built about 300 years ago and that young yews were planted beside it to dress the entrance. Over the centuries the trunks have grown against the stonework until they form part of the doorframe itself. The trouble with that tidy date is a note from 1897, when the Birmingham and Warwickshire Archaeological Society described the two ancient yew trees which seem to embrace the entrance as curious. Ancient, in 1897, sits awkwardly with a planting barely two centuries earlier, so we give the age as a broad band of 250 to 350 years and keep the dispute in view. Both are male trees. When the Ancient Yew Group measured them in 2006 they were 196 and 201 centimetres round at four feet, slim for churchyard yews, and Thomas Pakenham included them in Meetings with Remarkable Trees. The Tolkien connection is a rumour. The civic society uses that word, and the Diocese of Gloucester calls it unconfirmed. The door does not need it.

faq.q: Is the yew door at Stow-on-the-Wold really the Tolkien door?
faq.a: It is rumoured to have inspired the Doors of Durin in The Lord of the Rings, as Stow Civic Society puts it, but the link is unconfirmed. Nobody has documented Tolkien naming it.

faq.q: Where exactly is the door?
faq.a: On the north side of St Edward's Church on Church Street, a couple of minutes' walk from the Square. The churchyard is open and free.

painswick.intro: Painswick's churchyard is the reason most people stop in this Cotswold village. Around a hundred yews, clipped every September into rounded and pom-pom shapes, line the paths to St Mary's among a collection of chest tombs that starts in the early 17th century. Legend fixes the number at 99, because the Devil is said to kill any hundredth, and the count has never quite settled. The churchyard is open and free, and the Cotswold Way runs through the village.
painswick.meta_description: Legend says Painswick churchyard can only hold 99 yews. About a hundred clipped yews, their disputed count, their planting date and the September trim.
painswick.question_meta: How many yews are in Painswick churchyard? Legend says 99, the V&A counted 103, and the church plan shows 100. How old they are and when they are clipped.
painswick.question_answer: Painswick churchyard holds about a hundred clipped yews. Legend says there are 99 because the Devil destroys any hundredth, a hundredth was planted in 2000, the Victoria and Albert Museum once counted 103 and the church plan shows 100. Most were planted in the early 18th century, according to the National Trail.
painswick.question_context: The yews of St Mary's are not ancient trees but an ancient habit. The National Trail dates most of them to the early 18th century, about 300 years ago, while another account puts the planting in the 1790s, and the sources do not settle which is right. What has continued without a break is the clipping. Every September the yews are cut back into their rounded and pom-pom shapes, and more than two tons of clippings are collected each year. Fresh yew clippings are a source of paclitaxel, a drug used in cancer treatment. The number is the famous part. Folklore holds that only 99 yews will ever grow here, because the Devil will destroy a hundredth. In 2000, when parishes across the Diocese of Gloucester were given yews to mark the millennium, Painswick planted a hundredth. Counts since vary, from the church plan's 100 to the 103 recorded by the Victoria and Albert Museum, and the National Trail says more than 100. The Ancient Yew Group calls the churchyard an exceptional site. Count them yourself.

faq.q: When are the Painswick yews clipped?
faq.a: Every September, according to the National Trail. More than two tons of clippings are collected each year.

faq.q: How do I get to Painswick without a car?
faq.a: Stagecoach buses run from Stroud in about 20 minutes. Stroud station is about 6 km away, and the Cotswold Way passes through the village.

adlestrop.intro: Adlestrop's churchyard yew went unrecorded until 2012, when Lin Carter found it and the Ancient Yew Group came to measure. It turned out to be 6.33 metres round near the ground, a male yew in two trunks joined low down, by the west wall of St Mary Magdalene's churchyard. Someone has fitted a curved seat round its south side. The churchyard is open and free, in a small village a few kilometres from Moreton-in-Marsh.
adlestrop.meta_description: Nobody recorded the Adlestrop churchyard yew until 2012. It is 6.33 metres round near the ground, likely over 500 years old, and stands by the west wall.
adlestrop.question_meta: Adlestrop's oldest tree is a churchyard yew 6.33 metres round, first recorded in 2012 and likely over 500 years old by the Ancient Yew Group's girth bands.
adlestrop.question_answer: The oldest tree in Adlestrop is the yew in St Mary Magdalene's churchyard, 6.33 metres round near the ground. The Ancient Yew Group classes a yew this size as ancient, likely over 500 years old. That is an estimate from girth, not a dating, and the tree was only recorded in 2012.
adlestrop.question_context: For a tree of its size, the Adlestrop yew kept a remarkably low profile. It does not appear in the Ancient Yew Group's register until 2012, when Lin Carter came across it. Tim Hills then recorded a male yew of two trunks joined near the ground, the larger fragment about 14 feet round and the smaller about 10, both covered in ivy, with a combined girth of 20 feet 9 inches, or 633 centimetres, taken just above the ground. Peter Norton's 2017 visit repeated the figure. Hills judged that the two trunks look like sections of a once larger tree. Because the measurement is taken round both trunks at the base, it reads larger than a normal chest-height girth would. On the Group's banding, which puts yews of five to seven metres in its ancient class, the likely age is over 500 years. Nobody has dated it. The church beside it has a 14th or 15th century tower, and the rest of the building was rebuilt between 1750 and 1764.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Adlestrop churchyard?
faq.a: Close to the west wall of the churchyard, west of the tower, with a curved seat round its south and south-east side and a stone lean-to shed beside it.

faq.q: How do I get to Adlestrop?
faq.a: Moreton-in-Marsh is the nearest mainline station, roughly 6 km away. From there a car or taxi is the practical way.

coln-rogers.intro: Coln Rogers is a small village in the Coln valley north-east of Cirencester, and its church of St Andrew still has Saxon walls. In the churchyard, south-west of the building, grows a yew 5.74 metres round, which the Ancient Yew Group classes as ancient. Its measurements have barely moved between two recorders fourteen years apart. There is no railway, so come by car or bike, and the churchyard is open and free.
coln-rogers.meta_description: Beside the partly Saxon church of St Andrew in the Coln valley grows a yew 5.74 metres round, likely over 500 years old, its girth steady for 14 years.
coln-rogers.question_meta: Coln Rogers' oldest tree is the yew beside St Andrew's Saxon church, 5.74 metres round and likely over 500 years old by the Ancient Yew Group's bands.
coln-rogers.question_answer: The oldest tree in Coln Rogers is the yew south-west of St Andrew's church. The Ancient Yew Group records it at 574 centimetres round, which places it in their ancient class, likely over 500 years old. Nobody has dated it, so that age is an estimate from size.
coln-rogers.question_context: St Andrew's at Coln Rogers is a Grade I church, and parts of it are Saxon, from the 11th century on Wikipedia's dating. The yew in its churchyard has been measured by two people. Tim Hills visited in September 1999 and put it between 18 feet 6 and 19 feet 10 inches. Peter Norton came in 2013 and found 18 feet 10. The Ancient Yew Group's working figure is 574 centimetres, taken 30 centimetres above the ground. Across fourteen years the tree is essentially unchanged in size, which is what you would expect of an old yew and also why the tape is a poor clock. The Group places yews of five to seven metres in its ancient category, likely more than 500 years old, and that is the band we give. The pleasure here is the pairing of a Saxon church and an ancient yew in a quiet valley, a combination that takes a little finding and rewards the drive.

faq.q: Where is the yew at Coln Rogers?
faq.a: South-west of St Andrew's church, in its small churchyard. The church is Grade I and partly Saxon.

faq.q: Can I get to Coln Rogers by public transport?
faq.a: There is no railway, and we found no regular bus. A car, taxi or bike from Cirencester is the practical route.

hawling.intro: Hawling is a hamlet near Winchcombe, and the reason to come is a hollow female yew in the north-west corner of St Edward's churchyard, standing on the edge of a vertical drop to the old dairy. Three recorders have measured it across 26 years and found it barely changed, about 5.6 metres round. Arthur Mee called it gigantic in 1936; the tape says otherwise. There is no regular public transport, so plan to drive. The churchyard is open and free.
hawling.meta_description: Arthur Mee called the Hawling yew gigantic in 1936. Three recorders since found a hollow female tree about 5.6 metres round, likely over 500 years old.
hawling.question_meta: Hawling's oldest tree is a hollow female yew in St Edward's churchyard, about 5.6 metres round and likely over 500 years old by the Ancient Yew Group.
hawling.question_answer: The oldest tree in Hawling is the hollow female yew in the north-west corner of St Edward's churchyard, about 564 centimetres round. The Ancient Yew Group classes a yew this size as ancient, likely over 500 years old. That age is an estimate from girth; nobody has dated the tree.
hawling.question_context: The Hawling yew is one of the better measured trees in the Cotswolds. Allen Meredith put it at about 18 feet in 1988. Tim Hills recorded 549 centimetres at 30 centimetres up in 2003, and by 2014 the figure was between 18 feet and 18 feet 6, about 564 centimetres. Three people, 26 years and almost no change. In 1936 Arthur Mee wrote of a gigantic yew here, but Hills sees nothing to suggest it has been gigantic in recent times, so we stick to the measurements. It is a female tree with large hollow spaces and an opening on its north-west side, and Hills found it in vigorous good health in 2003. A younger female yew grows to its north-east. The church of St Edward is Grade II*, with sections from the early 13th century and a nave and chancel rebuilt in 1764. The yew stands at the edge of the churchyard where the ground drops away to the old dairy, which makes it easy to pick out.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Hawling churchyard?
faq.a: In the north-west corner of St Edward's churchyard, on the edge of a vertical drop to the old dairy. A younger yew grows to its north-east.

faq.q: Can I get to Hawling by bus?
faq.a: We found no regular public transport to Hawling. A car or taxi from Winchcombe is the practical way.

kemble.intro: Kemble's old yew grows only about two metres from the wall of All Saints church, and Kemble station, with direct services from London Paddington and Swindon, is about a kilometre away, so this is an ancient yew you can reach by train. The Ancient Yew Group classes it as ancient on its girth of about 4.9 metres. The churchyard is open and free.
kemble.meta_description: Kemble's ancient churchyard yew grows two metres from All Saints and a kilometre from the station, and old records make it look larger than it is.
kemble.question_meta: Kemble's oldest tree is the yew at All Saints church, about 4.9 metres round and several hundred years old by the Ancient Yew Group's girth bands.
kemble.question_answer: The oldest tree in Kemble is the yew in All Saints churchyard, growing about two metres from the church. Its modern girth is about 490 centimetres, which the Ancient Yew Group classes as ancient. The age estimate from that size is broad, several hundred years, roughly 300 to 600, with no dating behind it.
kemble.question_context: If you go back through the records, the Kemble yew seems to shrink. A Wiltshire archaeological journal gave 18 feet 6 inches, taken at six feet up, in 1894. Arthur Mee had 20 feet in 1938. Tim Hills measured 15 feet 8 in 1998 and 16 feet 1 in 2011, and Peter Norton found 16 feet 1 again at three and a half feet in 2015. The tree has not lost four feet of trunk. The older figures were taken at different heights, and on a yew the height you measure at changes the result a great deal. The modern readings agree at about 4.9 metres, and that is the figure we use. The Ancient Yew Group puts yews of four to five metres in its ancient class, and the age that implies is broad, somewhere between about 300 and 600 years. The Group's site file and photographs are dated 2026, so it is standing. It grows close to the church, about two metres from the wall.

faq.q: Can I reach the Kemble yew by train?
faq.a: Yes. Kemble station, with direct trains from London Paddington and Swindon, is about a kilometre from All Saints churchyard.

faq.q: Why do old records give a bigger girth?
faq.a: The 1894 and 1938 figures were measured at different heights on the trunk. Modern measurements, taken in 1998, 2011 and 2015, agree at about 4.9 metres.

compton-dundon.intro: Compton Dundon, a village near Street in Somerset, has a hollow male yew in the churchyard of St Andrew's that was already called very old in the 1780s. Edmund Rack measured it at 23 feet round then, and modern recorders find almost the same. It stands inside a low wall south-south-east of the church, in a churchyard that is open and free. Buses from Street and Somerton run through the village.
compton-dundon.meta_description: Edmund Rack measured the hollow Compton Dundon yew in the 1780s, and it has barely changed. Its disputed age and where it stands at St Andrew's.
compton-dundon.question_meta: Compton Dundon's oldest tree is the hollow yew at St Andrew's church, probably over 800 years old by the Ancient Yew Group, with claims up to 1,700.
compton-dundon.question_answer: The oldest tree in Compton Dundon is the hollow yew in St Andrew's churchyard, 742 centimetres round. The Ancient Yew Group's girth classes put it at probably over 800 years. Locally it was credited with about 1,000 years in 1954, and Wikipedia says over 1,700, but none of these is a dating.
compton-dundon.question_context: Few churchyard yews have a measurement as old as this one. Edmund Rack, who died in 1787, surveyed the churchyard and described a very old yew with a fine top, its body hollow and measuring 23 feet in circumference. Two centuries later Tim Hills recorded 24 feet 9 inches at ground level in 2000, and Peter Norton found 23 feet 9 in 2014. The Ancient Yew Group's figure is 742 centimetres, taken 30 centimetres above the ground. The ages offered for it vary a great deal. The Group's girth classes put a yew of this size at probably over 800 years, which is an estimate from size. In 1954 the Rev. R. Kelland recorded that it was locally credited with about 1,000 years. Wikipedia gives over 1,700 years without a source. We report all three, and the plain conclusion that it is very old and has never been dated. It is a male tree, still hollow, and it stands inside a low wall south-south-east of the church.

faq.q: Where is the yew at Compton Dundon?
faq.a: Inside a low wall south-south-east of St Andrew's church, in the open churchyard.

faq.q: Can I get there by bus?
faq.a: Buses between Street and Somerton run through Compton Dundon; check the current timetable. There is no railway.

ashbrittle.intro: Ashbrittle is a remote hilltop village west of Wellington in Somerset, and its yew grows on a grassy mound south-east of the church of St John the Baptist that may be a Bronze Age barrow. It measures 12.17 metres round near the ground, and in 2002 it was named one of 50 Great British Trees. There is no regular bus, so plan to drive. The churchyard is open and free.
ashbrittle.meta_description: Ashbrittle's yew, 12.17 metres round, grows on a mound that may be a Bronze Age barrow. One of 50 Great British Trees, with its disputed age.
ashbrittle.question_meta: Ashbrittle's ancient yew, 12.17 metres round, is over 1,000 years old on the Ancient Yew Group's banding. Claims of 3,000 years and more are undated.
ashbrittle.question_answer: The oldest tree in Ashbrittle is the yew in the churchyard of St John the Baptist, 12.17 metres round near the ground. The Ancient Yew Group's banding puts a yew this size at over 1,000 years. Popular claims of 3,000 years or more are repeated widely but rest on no dating.
ashbrittle.question_context: The Ashbrittle yew grows on a tumulus about one and a half metres high and fifteen metres across, south-east of the church. The mound is thought possibly to be a Bronze Age barrow, but that is unproven, and a few headstones stand around its edge. The Ancient Yew Group recorded the girth as 12.17 metres, measured five centimetres above the ground, and holds photographs of the tree from 1848, 1997 and 2014. Its age is where the stories outrun the evidence. Wikipedia repeats a belief that it is over 3,000 years old, and other claims go further. None of them comes from a dating, so we give the Group's girth band of over 1,000 years and leave the rest as folklore. The folklore is lively. Childless couples who visit its base are said to conceive within a year. In 2002 the Tree Council made it one of 50 Great British Trees for the Golden Jubilee. The Church Times reported it looking under the weather in 2015, and it was still standing then.

faq.q: How old is the Ashbrittle yew?
faq.a: Nobody has dated it. The Ancient Yew Group's girth banding puts a yew of 12.17 metres at over 1,000 years. Claims of 3,000 years or more are popular but undated.

faq.q: How do I get to Ashbrittle?
faq.a: It is a remote hilltop village west of Wellington with no railway, and we found no regular bus. Driving is the practical way.

kingston-st-mary.intro: Kingston St Mary is a village just north of Taunton, and south-west of its Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary stands a yew that split apart long ago. Its hollow trunk has divided into four fragments that now stand as separate trunks in a ring, 10.03 metres round at the ground. Nobody has found an early written record of it. The churchyard is open and free, with a local bus from Taunton.
kingston-st-mary.meta_description: Near Taunton, the Kingston St Mary yew has split into four trunks standing in a ring 10.03 metres round, with no early record of it found anywhere.
kingston-st-mary.question_meta: Kingston St Mary's oldest tree is a split yew, four trunks in a ring 10.03 metres round, in the Ancient Yew Group's top girth class of seven metres.
kingston-st-mary.question_answer: The oldest tree in Kingston St Mary is the yew south-west of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a hollow tree split into four trunks with a ring 10.03 metres round at ground level. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class, seven metres and over. Nobody has dated it.
kingston-st-mary.question_context: When Tim Hills recorded this yew in 2001, the ancient trunk had long since been divided by its hollow into four fragments, which now stand as separate trunks and were full of ivy at the time. Measured round the whole ring at ground level, it came to 10.03 metres, and Wondermondo gives the same figure. Because that is the girth of a circle of fragments rather than of one stem, it describes the footprint of the old tree, not the width of any single trunk. The Ancient Yew Group classes yews of seven metres and over as ancient, with an age band starting at about 800 years. That is an estimate from size, not a dating. Unusually for a yew this big, the Group found no early reference to it at all. The church dates from about 1225, so the tree has had eight centuries of neighbours who apparently never wrote it down. Photographs were updated in 2016. If you know an older mention, in a parish history, a painting or a letter, tell us.

faq.q: Why does the Kingston St Mary yew have four trunks?
faq.a: Its trunk hollowed and split into four fragments that now stand apart. The 10.03 metre girth is measured round the whole ring.

faq.q: How do I get there?
faq.a: A local bus runs from Taunton to Kingston St Mary; check the timetable. There is no railway.

broadwindsor.intro: Broadwindsor, between Beaminster and Crewkerne in west Dorset, has a yew of about 15 stems rising from a raised mound east of the church of St John the Baptist. A photograph from 1867, the time of the church's restoration, shows what may be a stump in its place, which suggests the tree was once cut back and came back many times over. The churchyard is open and free. The bus is infrequent, so most visitors drive.
broadwindsor.meta_description: Victorian restorers may have cut the Broadwindsor yew to a stump. It came back as about 15 stems on a mound east of the church, 10.34 metres round.
broadwindsor.question_meta: Broadwindsor's oldest tree is a multi-stemmed yew on a mound east of St John the Baptist's church, in the Ancient Yew Group's top class at 10.34 metres.
broadwindsor.question_answer: The oldest tree in Broadwindsor is the yew east of the church of St John the Baptist, about 15 stems on a raised mound with a combined girth of 10.34 metres at ground level. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over. Nobody has dated it.
broadwindsor.question_context: The Broadwindsor yew is a puzzle the Ancient Yew Group has left open. A photograph taken in 1867, during the church's restoration, shows a stump-like tree where it stands, and the Group asks whether the yew was cut back to a stump at that time. What grows there now is a cluster of about 15 stems on a mound east of the church, counted in 1998. Wondermondo gives each trunk as between 0.9 and 1.8 metres round and the mound as about 1.2 metres high. The girth of 10.34 metres is taken round the whole mass at ground level, so it overstates any one stem, and a 1994 book gave 33 feet. The Group classes yews over seven metres as ancient, an estimate from size rather than a date. The tree is male. Its health was recorded as below average in 2015, and it was photographed again in 2024. The church of St John the Baptist dates from about 1180.

faq.q: Why does the Broadwindsor yew have so many stems?
faq.a: It may have been cut back to a stump during the church's restoration in 1867 or 1868 and regrown as about 15 stems, though the Ancient Yew Group treats this as an open question.

faq.q: Is there public transport to Broadwindsor?
faq.a: There is an infrequent bus; check before you travel. Most visitors drive.

woolland.intro: Woolland is a hamlet in Dorset's Blackmore Vale, between Blandford Forum and Sturminster Newton, and south of its small 1855 church stands a great stout yew about 9.5 metres round near the ground. Its girth has barely changed since 1944. The church stands on an early Saxon site, and one yew writer suggested the tree may have sheltered three or four churches. There is no practical public transport, so plan to drive. The churchyard is open and free.
woolland.meta_description: Measured at 31 feet 4 inches in 1944 and 31 feet 1 in 2012, the Woolland yew in the Blackmore Vale stands beside an 1855 church on an early Saxon site.
woolland.question_meta: Woolland's oldest tree is the stout churchyard yew south of the 1855 church, in the Ancient Yew Group's top class at 9.47 metres round.
woolland.question_answer: The oldest tree in Woolland is the yew south of the 1855 church, 947 centimetres round near the ground when Peter Norton measured it in 2012. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over, an estimate from size. Nobody has dated it.
woolland.question_context: The Woolland yew has been measured for more than seventy years. In 1944 it was measured at 31 feet 4 inches for Vaughan Cornish's book The Churchyard Yew and Immortality. In 1998 it was 31 feet at one foot up, and in 2012 Peter Norton found 947 centimetres at 30 centimetres, or 31 feet 1. Seventy years, and almost no change. The church beside it was built in 1855 on an early Saxon site. Baxter's book The Eternal Yew, as quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, suggests it may be the only yew to have sheltered three or four churches, a claim from one writer rather than a record. The Group classes yews of seven metres and over as ancient, and that is an estimate from girth, not a date. It was photographed again in 2026. Woolland itself is a small hamlet in the Blackmore Vale with no practical bus, so a car is the realistic way to get here.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Woolland?
faq.a: South of the small church of 1855, in the open churchyard.

faq.q: Has the Woolland yew grown since it was first measured?
faq.a: Barely. It was 31 feet 4 inches in 1944 and 31 feet 1 inch, or 947 centimetres, in 2012.

wimborne-st-giles.intro: Wimborne St Giles lies north of Wimborne Minster in Dorset, and its churchyard sits beside the entrance to St Giles Park. The big male yew east-south-east of the church divides at about eight feet into six large limbs round a huge central branch. It first appeared in print in 1884, when Lord Shaftesbury pointed it out to The Quiver. A slimmer columnar yew grows to its south-east. The churchyard is open and free.
wimborne-st-giles.meta_description: Lord Shaftesbury pointed out the Wimborne St Giles yew in 1884. Six great limbs round one central branch, 7.21 metres round, and how to find it.
wimborne-st-giles.question_meta: Wimborne St Giles' oldest tree is the male yew east-south-east of St Giles church, 7.21 metres round at chest height, first recorded in 1884.
wimborne-st-giles.question_answer: The oldest tree in Wimborne St Giles is the big yew east-south-east of St Giles church, 721 centimetres round at 120 centimetres up. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its ancient class of seven metres and over, an estimate from size. It was first mentioned in 1884, in the magazine The Quiver.
wimborne-st-giles.question_context: This yew owes its first appearance in print to Lord Shaftesbury, who pointed it out to The Quiver in 1884. Peter Andrews measured it for the Ancient Yew Group in 2006 at 721 centimetres, taken at 120 centimetres up, close to chest height, where many churchyard yew figures are taken much nearer the ground. It is a male tree, and its shape is distinctive. At about eight feet the trunk divides into six large limbs that stand round one huge central branch. The Group classes yews over seven metres as ancient, which is an estimate from girth and not a dating. The church beside it was rebuilt in the 18th century, and the churchyard sits next to the entrance to St Giles Park. It was photographed again in 2026. One thing to watch for is the second yew. A slimmer, columnar male tree grows to the south-east, about 3.4 metres round at two feet. The ancient one is the broad, many-limbed tree east-south-east of the church.

faq.q: Which yew is the old one at Wimborne St Giles?
faq.a: The broad yew east-south-east of the church, branching into six big limbs at about eight feet. The slim columnar yew to the south-east is a different, smaller tree.

faq.q: How do I get to Wimborne St Giles?
faq.a: It is a village north of Wimborne Minster. A bus serves the area; check the timetable, or drive.

lytchett-matravers.intro: Lytchett Matravers is a village north-west of Poole, and by the north door of its Grade I church of St Mary the Virgin stands an old yew 6.48 metres round, first recorded in a Post Office Directory of 1855. A much younger yew grows nearby and is easy to mistake for it. The churchyard is open and free, with a local bus from Poole, though driving is easier.
lytchett-matravers.meta_description: First recorded in an 1855 Post Office Directory, the Lytchett Matravers yew stands by the north door of St Mary the Virgin, probably over 600 years old.
lytchett-matravers.question_meta: Lytchett Matravers' oldest tree is the yew by the north door of St Mary the Virgin, probably over 600 years old on the Ancient Yew Group's girth classes.
lytchett-matravers.question_answer: The oldest tree in Lytchett Matravers is the yew north-west of St Mary the Virgin church, by the north door, 648 centimetres round. The Ancient Yew Group classes yews of five to seven metres as probably over 600 years old. Claims of 1,600 years are undated.
lytchett-matravers.question_context: The earliest written mention of the Lytchett Matravers yew is in the Post Office Directory of 1855. Tim Hills recorded it in 1999 at 21 feet 3 and 21 feet 10 inches just above five feet, and the Ancient Yew Group's current figure is 648 centimetres at 30 centimetres off the ground. On the Group's banding, a yew of five to seven metres is probably more than 600 years old. That is an estimate from girth. You will find bolder figures elsewhere, a blog claim of 1,600 years and a planting date of AD 590 mentioned by the National Churches Trust, but neither comes with a dating, and we do not use them. The church of St Mary the Virgin is Grade I and dates from about 1200. The yew grows on its north-west side, beside the north door. A much younger yew grows close by, 11 feet 10 inches round in 2011, big enough to be mistaken for the old one. The ancient tree is roughly twice its girth.

faq.q: Which is the old yew at Lytchett Matravers?
faq.a: The larger yew by the north door, north-west of the church, about 6.5 metres round. A younger yew nearby is about 3.6 metres round.

faq.q: Is the Lytchett Matravers yew 1,600 years old?
faq.a: That figure is a popular claim without a dating. The Ancient Yew Group's girth class puts it at probably over 600 years.

dinder.intro: Dinder is a village about four kilometres east of Wells, and south-east of its church of St Michael and All Angels grows a yew 9.12 metres round at the ground. The Ancient Yew Group puts it in its top class. Its one old description, from an 1857 guide, may actually belong to the yew at Dunster. The churchyard is open and free, and a bus runs from Wells.
dinder.meta_description: Four kilometres from Wells, the Dinder yew is 9.12 metres round at the ground, and its one old description may belong to a tree at Dunster.
dinder.question_meta: Dinder's oldest tree is the yew south-east of St Michael and All Angels, 9.12 metres round at the ground, a short trip from Wells.
dinder.question_answer: The oldest tree in Dinder is the yew south-east of the church of St Michael and All Angels, 912 centimetres round at ground level. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over, which it treats as ancient. That is an estimate from girth; nobody has dated it.
dinder.question_context: Tim Hills measured the Dinder yew at 912 centimetres at ground level in 1997, and Peter Norton photographed it in 2015. Beyond that, its written history is thin and possibly borrowed. An 1857 Guide to Minehead and Its Environs, quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, describes a yew of great age and formerly of considerable extent. The Group gives the identical sentence for the yew at Dunster, so the line probably cannot be relied on for Dinder at all. The Group classes yews over seven metres as ancient, an estimate from size rather than a date. The church of St Michael and All Angels is Grade II* and may stand on a Saxon site. Dinder is four kilometres east of Wells, close enough to fit around a visit to the city, and a bus runs between the two. If you know of an old record that names this tree and not Dunster's, tell us.

faq.q: How far is Dinder from Wells?
faq.a: About four kilometres east. A bus runs from Wells; check the timetable.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Dinder churchyard?
faq.a: South-east of the church of St Michael and All Angels.

combe-florey.intro: Combe Florey, a village north-west of Taunton, has two female yews in the churchyard of St Peter and St Paul. The young one grows north-west of the church. The ancient one stands south of it on the east side, 8.13 metres round near the ground, in the Ancient Yew Group's top class. The church dates from about 1300 and is Grade I. The churchyard is open and free, and the Taunton to Williton bus passes along the A358.
combe-florey.meta_description: Two female yews share the churchyard at Combe Florey near Taunton, one young and one ancient, 8.13 metres round, south of a Grade I church.
combe-florey.question_meta: Combe Florey's oldest tree is the ancient female yew south of St Peter and St Paul church, 8.13 metres round, in the Ancient Yew Group's top class.
combe-florey.question_answer: The oldest tree in Combe Florey is the female yew south of the church of St Peter and St Paul, on its east side, 813 centimetres round five centimetres above the ground. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over. Nobody has dated it.
combe-florey.question_context: The churchyard at Combe Florey holds two yews, both female, and they make a useful pair. The ancient one stands south of the church on the east side, and the Ancient Yew Group measured it at 813 centimetres, taken five centimetres above the ground, where a yew's trunk is at its widest. Its photograph was updated in 2015. The young one grows north-west of the church. The Group puts yews over seven metres in its ancient class, an estimate from size rather than a dating, so the age stays open. The church of St Peter and St Paul dates from about 1300 and is Grade I. Female yews are the ones that carry red, fleshy cups around their seeds in autumn; male trees only shed pollen. The Ancient Yew Group is the one source for the tree itself, so its size and age band come from their record. The village lies north-west of Taunton, and the Taunton to Williton bus runs along the A358 close by.

faq.q: Which is the ancient yew at Combe Florey?
faq.a: The larger yew south of the church, on its east side. A young yew grows north-west of the church.

faq.q: Can I get to Combe Florey by bus?
faq.a: The Taunton to Williton bus along the A358 passes the village; check the timetable. There is no railway.

chilcompton.intro: Chilcompton, a village near Midsomer Norton in Somerset, has the one ancient yew the Diocese of Bath and Wells listed in this parish in 2013. It stands south-west of the church of St John the Baptist, 7.8 metres round at the root crown. The most recent photograph we know of dates from 2006, so a visitor's picture would be welcome. The churchyard is open and free, with buses from Midsomer Norton and Bath.
chilcompton.meta_description: The Diocese of Bath and Wells counted one ancient yew at Chilcompton, 7.8 metres round at the root crown. Where it stands and how to reach it by bus.
chilcompton.question_meta: Chilcompton's oldest tree is the yew south-west of St John the Baptist's church, 7.8 metres round, the parish's only ancient yew on the diocese list.
chilcompton.question_answer: The oldest tree in Chilcompton is the yew south-west of the church of St John the Baptist, 780 centimetres round at the root crown. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over, and the Diocese of Bath and Wells listed it as the parish's one ancient yew in 2013. Nobody has dated it.
chilcompton.question_context: Tim Hills recorded the Chilcompton yew at 780 centimetres at the root crown, the point where the trunk flares into its roots, and photographed it in 2006. That girth places it in the Ancient Yew Group's top class, seven metres and over, which the Group treats as ancient. As with every age read from a tape, that is an estimate from size and not a dating. The Diocese of Bath and Wells, in its list of ancient yews, counted one ancient yew in this churchyard in 2013. The tree stands south-west of St John the Baptist, a church on the northern edge of the village. There is one gap. The latest photograph we have found is from 2006, and we have no more recent sighting. If you visit, a photograph of the tree would settle the question for everyone who comes after you. Buses run to Chilcompton from Midsomer Norton and from Bath, so this one is reachable without a car.

faq.q: Is the Chilcompton yew still standing?
faq.a: The latest photograph we know of is from 2006 and the diocese listed it in 2013. We have no more recent sighting, so a visitor's photograph would help.

faq.q: How do I get to Chilcompton?
faq.a: Buses run from Midsomer Norton and Bath; check the current timetable.

exeter.intro: Exeter's two old yews are a short city trip and a longer country one. The Heavitree yew stands by the church door of St Michael and All Angels, about two kilometres east of the centre, and a local guide calls it the oldest tree in Exeter. The Kenn yew is about nine kilometres south-west of the city by road, in St Andrew's churchyard, and at over ten metres round it is far bigger. Both churchyards are open and free.
exeter.meta_description: Exeter has two ancient yews worth the trip, the Heavitree yew by its church door and the 10.56 metre Kenn yew nine kilometres out of the city.
exeter.question_meta: The oldest tree in Exeter is the Heavitree yew, thought to be over 500 years old. Nine kilometres out, the Kenn yew is claimed at over 1,000 years.
exeter.question_answer: Inside the city, the oldest tree in Exeter is the Heavitree yew in the churchyard of St Michael and All Angels, which the local guide Exeter Trees and Shrubs says is thought to be over 500 years old. About nine kilometres south-west, the Kenn yew is far larger and claimed at over 1,000 years, though neither has been dated.
exeter.question_context: The Heavitree yew is small for its reputation. Tim Hills recorded it at 307 centimetres at ground level in 2004, yet the Tree Council named it one of 50 Great British Trees for the Golden Jubilee in 2002, and Exeter Trees and Shrubs calls it the oldest tree in the city. There has been a church on the site since at least 1152, and the Ancient Yew Group notes the old idea that Heavitree was named for a heafod treow, a head tree where Saxon kings held court, while saying it will never be known whether this yew was it. In 2019 the council arranged to lift tarmac and loosen the soil over its roots after vehicles had driven across them. The Kenn yew, in St Andrew's churchyard about nine kilometres from the centre, is a different scale of tree, 10.56 metres round at ground level in 1999. The church says the Conservation Foundation certified it as over 1,000 years old, and the yew expert Allen Meredith thinks it nearer 2,000. Neither is a dating. A notice board at the tree calls it among the oldest in England.

faq.q: How do I get to the Heavitree yew?
faq.a: Heavitree is about two kilometres east of Exeter city centre. The yew stands near the door of St Michael and All Angels, off Church Street, in a free public churchyard.

faq.q: Is the Kenn yew in Exeter?
faq.a: No. Kenn is a village about nine kilometres south-west of Exeter city centre by road. Check for a bus before you go, or come by car or bike.

dartmoor.intro: Wistman's Wood is the oak wood Dartmoor is famous for, about 3.5 hectares of low, twisted, moss-covered oaks among granite boulders above the West Dart, north of Two Bridges. Its oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old, and most stand no taller than 4.5 metres. It is a National Nature Reserve, and visitors are asked to stay on the paths around the edge and not to enter the wood. The walk from the Two Bridges car park takes about 25 minutes.
dartmoor.meta_description: Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor holds oaks 400 to 500 years old that rarely pass 4.5 metres. About 120 lichens, why it is seen from the path, and the walk in.
dartmoor.question_meta: How old is Wistman's Wood? Its oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old. Why they stay so low, what grows on them, and how to see it from the path.
dartmoor.question_answer: The oldest oaks in Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor appear to be 400 to 500 years old, according to Wikipedia's summary of the research. Most are no more than 4.5 metres tall. The wood covers about 3.5 hectares and is seen from the paths around its edge, since visitors are asked not to enter it.
dartmoor.question_context: Wistman's Wood grows at 380 to 410 metres on the open moor in the valley of the West Dart, in three groves known as North, Middle and South. Around 1620 it was described as oaks no taller than a man could reach the top of with his head, and most still rarely exceed 4.5 metres, with a few between six and 7.6. The oldest appear to be 400 to 500 years old, and an oak felled in 1866 proved to be about 168. Wikipedia describes the trees as mainly pedunculate oak with some rowan, while one walking guide calls them sessile. What makes the wood precious is less the oaks than what lives on them and on the boulders, about 120 species of lichen among the mosses. Feet damage both, which is why Natural England and the Dartmoor National Park Authority ask visitors to keep to the paths around the edge. The wood has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1964 and belongs to the Duchy of Cornwall. A 2023 plan aims to reduce grazing and foot traffic and expand the wood by 2040.

faq.q: Can you walk into Wistman's Wood?
faq.a: Natural England and the Dartmoor National Park Authority ask visitors to follow the paths around the wood and not to enter it, because erosion damages the lichens and mosses. The view from the path at its edge is the way to see it.

faq.q: How do I get to Wistman's Wood?
faq.a: Park at Two Bridges on the B3357, opposite the Two Bridges Hotel, and walk north for about 25 minutes.
